Learning Objectives
Review the clinical and radiographic characteristics of femoral neck fractures in young adults.
Describe classification systems for femoral neck fractures.
Explain methods of reduction and fixation of femoral neck fractures in young adults based on
their unique fracture patterns.
Review the pathophysiology and management of complications associated with femoral neck
fractures in young adults.


Overview
Femoral neck fractures in young adults are devastating injuries that typically result from
high-energy trauma. Fractures are classified based on the degree of displacement and
orientation of the fracture plane. Goals of treatment for young adults are to restore
native anatomy, preserve the joint, and enable return to preinjury level of function.
Acute management involves anatomic reduction and stable fixation. Even with ideal
fixation, complications, such as osteonecrosis, malunion, and nonunion, are common
and may lead to revision surgery (Figure 1).
Figure 1 AP radiographs of the hip of a 17-year-old boy injured in a motorcycle collision
demonstrate the injury (A), fracture repair (B), loss of fixation and nonunion at 4 months
postoperatively (C), and results of a proximal femoral osteotomy 1 year after revision
surgery (D). (Reproduced from Collinge C, Mir H: Femoral neck fractures in the younger
patient, in Ricci WM, Ostrum RF, eds: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Trauma, ed 5.
Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2016, pp 465-473.)
Epidemiology/Etiology
Femoral neck fractures are less common in young adults than in geriatric patients.
These injuries result from high-energy trauma, most commonly motor vehicle collisions or falls
from a substantial height.

Epidemiology/Etiology

Femoral neck fractures in young adults usually result from high-energy mechanisms of
injury. These patients should be resuscitated according to Advanced Trauma Life
Support protocol and medically optimized before surgical fixation. More than 250,000
femoral neck fractures occur annually; however, most of these fractures occur in older
patients after low-energy trauma. Femoral neck fractures in young adults are associated
with more comminution and displacement compared with femoral neck fractures in the
elderly. These injuries are particularly challenging because of the high rate of
complications, regardless of treatment strategy.
Anatomy
Osteology
The mean femoral neck-shaft angle is 130° with 15° of anteversion (Figure 2).
The proximal femur consists of cortical and cancellous bone. The strongest is bone located in
the posteromedial neck, termed the calcar.
Femoral neck fractures are intracapsular fractures and are associated with a higher risk of
nonunion.
Radiographs of the contralateral hip may help determine the accuracy of reduction.

Osteology
The mean adult femoral neck-shaft angle is 130° (± 7°) with 10° (± 7°) of anteversion.1-3
These angles are variable; therefore, radiographs of the uninjured side aid in
understanding a patient’s native anatomy. The anatomy of the proximal femur is
complex. The two prime trabecular groups of the proximal femur are the principal
tensile group and the principal compressive group. Secondary compressive and tensile
trabecular groups also exist. These trabecular bone patterns are the result of bone
response to stress, expressed as the Wolff law. The weakest area in the femoral neck is
the Ward triangle. The calcar is a medial area of dense trabecular bone that transfers
stress from the femoral shaft to the inferior portion of the femoral neck. A patient’s

native anatomy should be restored after reduction and fixation. Varus alignment should
be avoided.
Vascular Anatomy
Knowledge of the blood supply to the femoral head is crucial.
The major blood supply to the femoral head is the medial femoral circumflex artery. The
terminal branches of this vessel often are disrupted during high-energy injuries with
substantial fracture displacement (Figure 3).
Additional vascular contributions come from the lateral femoral circumflex artery and the
obturator artery.
Disruption of the blood supply to the femoral head during femoral neck fracture is a
considerable factor in the development of osteonecrosis.
Figure 3 Anterior (A) and posterior (B) view illustrations show the vascular anatomy of the
femoral neck. (Reproduced with permission from Goldstein C, Bhandari M: Femoral neck
fractures. Musculoskeletal Key. June 7, 2016. Available at: https://musculoskeletalkey.com/17-
femoral-neck-fractures/. Accessed January 27, 2023.)

An understanding of the blood supply to the femoral head is crucial for proper
management of femoral neck fractures in young adults. The main blood supply to the
femoral head is based posteriorly via the medial femoral circumflex artery. The medial
femoral circumflex artery supplies 82% of the femoral head and 67% of the femoral
neck. The vessel travels anterior to the piriformis before coursing up the
posterosuperior femoral neck.4 It branches into intraosseous nutrient vessels and
delicate retinacular vessels that course the surface of the femoral neck superiorly to the
femoral head and are completely intracapsular.5,6 Additional contributions come from
the lateral femoral circumflex artery and the obturator artery. The terminal branches of
these vessels form a complex anastomosis around the femoral head, and damage to
these vessels during injury or fracture manipulation plays an integral role in the
development of osteonecrosis. Venous congestion may be caused by increased
intracapsular pressure secondary to the fracture hematoma. Insufficient evidence
supports a hip capsulotomy to decrease intracapsular pressure.
Injury Classification
Femoral neck fractures are classified based on anatomic location, displacement, and
orientation of the fracture plane.
Femoral neck fractures can be described as subcapital, transcervical, and basicervical based on
their anatomic location.
The Garden classification divides fractures into four groups based on displacement. More
commonly, fractures are simply described as displaced or nondisplaced because this is more
relevant for treatment decisions and prognosis (Figure 4).
The Pauwels classification describes fractures based on the orientation of the fracture plane
relative to a horizontal reference line. Fractures with a lower Pauwels angle are subjected to
more compressive forces. Fractures with a higher Pauwels angle are subjected to higher shear
forces (Figure 5).

Injury Classification

7/29

Multiple classification systems have been developed to describe femoral neck fractures
based on fracture location, displacement, and orientation. These descriptive systems
have implications for management and prognosis. Descriptors, including subcapital,
transcervical, and basicervical, refer to the location of the fracture line in the proximal or
distal neck. The Garden classification system, developed in 1961, divides fractures into
four groups based on the degree of displacement. A type I fracture is incomplete, or
valgus impacted. A type II fracture is complete but nondisplaced. A type III fracture is
complete with partial displacement, and a type IV fracture is completely displaced. In
practice, the Garden system is more clinically useful if used to discern nondisplaced and
valgus impacted fractures (Garden type I and type II) from displaced fractures (Garden
type III and type IV). Nondisplaced fractures can be fixed in situ, whereas displaced
fractures require reduction. Overall, displaced fractures result in more complications
than nondisplaced fractures.
The Pauwels classification system is used to describe the orientation of the fracture
plane relative to a horizontal reference line: type I fractures are less than 30°, type II
fractures are between 30° and 50°, and type III fractures are greater than 50°.7 Fractures
with a higher Pauwels angle are subject to more shear forces, whereas fractures with a
lower Pauwels angle are subject to more compressive forces.8 Fractures with a large
Pauwels angle (type III) or with substantial displacement are inherently less stable and
prone to osteonecrosis and nonunion.9
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History/Physical Examination
The mechanism and timing of the injury must be determined because this may affect the
urgency of surgical management and suggest other associated injuries.
Patients with a femoral neck fracture commonly present with pain located in the groin, thigh,
or lateral hip.
Patients with a displaced fracture are unable to ambulate, and the extremity is shortened
and/or externally rotated.
Because these injuries typically result from high-energy mechanisms, all patients should
undergo a secondary survey to evaluate for additional injuries.


Patient History/Physical Examination
The diagnosis and initial treatment of patients in whom a femoral neck fracture is
suspected involves a detailed history, physical examination, and understanding of the
mechanism of injury. Surgeons must understand how and when the injury occurred
because this may affect the urgency of surgical management and suggest other
associated injuries. In patients who sustain high-energy trauma, a complete
musculoskeletal and visceral trauma workup should be performed. Patients typically
describe pain in the groin and thigh, and the involved extremity is shortened and
externally rotated. Patients may be distracted by other injuries or present with altered
mental status. Therefore, clinical suspicion should be high in any patient with high-
energy trauma, regardless of the patient’s initial complaints.
Imaging Studies
Workup for any patient in whom a femoral neck fracture is suspected should include AP pelvis,
AP hip, and cross-table lateral radiographs.
A traction/internal rotation view may help delineate the fracture fragments because it
eliminates anteversion and profiles the entire femoral neck.
A fine-cut CT scan may aid fracture characterization and preoperative planning (Figure 6).

Imaging Studies
Imaging studies for patients in whom a femoral neck fracture is suspected begins with
plain radiographs, specifically an AP view of the pelvis and AP and cross-table lateral
views of the affected hip. A frog-leg lateral view is contraindicated because it may cause
displacement of a previously nondisplaced or impacted fracture. Radiographs of the
entire femur should be obtained to recognize any deformity or concomitant injury that
may alter fixation methods. A traction/internal rotation view may better characterize a
displaced fracture pattern because it eliminates femoral anteversion and better profiles
the femoral neck. If marked fracture shortening is present, repeat radiographs obtained
after the application of skeletal traction may aid in fracture classification. In addition, a
CT scan typically is obtained for preoperative planning. It often shows additional
comminution in the posterior caudal neck that may be difficult to appreciate with
radiographs alone.10 CT scans also may be useful in confirming a suspected minimally
displaced fracture.

Associated Injuries
Femoral neck fractures may occur in isolation but often occur in combination with femoral
shaft, femoral head, pelvic ring, and acetabular injuries.
Femoral neck fractures occur in combination with 1% to 9% of high-energy, blunt femoral shaft
fractures. Many of these femoral neck fractures are nondisplaced on presentation and missed
on initial assessment.
A fine-cut CT scan should be obtained in all patients with a femoral shaft fracture to
thoroughly evaluate the femoral neck.
Recognition and management of nondisplaced femoral neck fractures in patients with an
ipsilateral femoral shaft fracture is critical in preventing displacement, osteonecrosis, and
nonunion.

Associated Injuries
Femoral neck fractures are commonly associated with blunt femoral shaft fractures;
however, many studies report high rates of late diagnosis of femoral neck fractures in
these patients. Approximately 25% to 60% of these femoral neck fractures are
nondisplaced on presentation, and many are missed on the initial assessment. Tornetta
et al11 developed a protocol to increase the rate of diagnosis of these injuries. This
includes a preoperative AP internal rotation radiograph of the hip, a fine-cut (2 mm) CT
scan through the femoral neck, and intraoperative fluoroscopic evaluation before
fixation of the femoral neck. After initiation of this protocol, delayed diagnosis of femoral
neck fractures was reduced by 91% (Resource 1).
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Surgical fixation is recommended for almost all patients, except those who are nonambulatory
or too ill to undergo surgical treatment.
Nondisplaced fractures in young adults are stabilized in situ to prevent displacement.
Outcomes are highly correlated with anatomic reduction and stable fixation.

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002100
11/29

Fixation becomes more difficult and rates of complications increase in patients with late
displacement or malunion.

Nonsurgical Management
The treatment goals for femoral neck fractures in young adults are achieving union with
anatomic alignment while avoiding osteonecrosis. Surgical management is indicated for
nondisplaced, minimally displaced, and completely displaced injures. Stable fixation
restores anatomy, allows for early mobilization, and decreases the risk of nonunion and
malunion. These complications require a salvage procedure, such as a corrective
osteotomy or total hip arthroplasty.
Surgical Management
Indications
The goal of femoral neck fracture management in young adults is to restore patients to their
preoperative level of function, preserve the native joint, and minimize complications.
Nondisplaced fractures are managed via in situ fixation.
Displaced fractures are managed via open reduction and internal fixation. The most commonly
used implants are multiple parallel interfragmentary screws and/or a sliding hip screw (SHS);
however, various other options exist.
The literature does not support clear superiority of a single fixation construct. A patient’s
fracture pattern, bone quality, and concomitant injuries all must be considered in planning the
surgical strategy.

Indications
Achieving anatomic reduction and stable fixation is critical to successful union and good
functional results. Multiple studies have shown that initial displacement and quality of
femoral neck reduction are predictors of outcomes. Nondisplaced neck fractures are
managed via in situ fixation. Displaced fractures are managed via closed and/or open

reduction and internal fixation. The most commonly used implants are multiple parallel
interfragmentary screws and/or a SHS; however, many other options exist. Because of
persistently high complication rates, newer implants that combine the mechanical
strengths of fixed-angle devices with the sliding advantages of screw fixation are
emerging. Various femoral neck–specific implants have been introduced with mixed
results. The literature does not support the superiority of any fixation device. A patient’s
fracture pattern, bone quality, and concomitant injuries must be considered in planning
the surgical strategy.
Surgical Timing
The timing of surgical treatment for young adults with a femoral neck fracture is somewhat
controversial.
Historically, emergent reduction and fixation was performed with the notion that it improved
perfusion of the femoral head and decreased rates of osteonecrosis.
Contemporary studies have shown that time to fixation is not a predictor of complications
after internal fixation of femoral neck fractures in young adults.
Current recommendations are that surgical management be performed within 24 to 48 hours
in a medically stable patient and with an appropriately trained surgical team.

Surgical Timing
Historically, management of displaced femoral neck fractures was viewed as an
emergent procedure, and efforts were made to reduce and stabilize these fractures
within 12 hours postinjury. Reduction of the fracture was thought to minimize the risk of
continued damage to the remaining vascular supply and decrease the rate of
osteonecrosis, malunion, and nonunion.12-16 Initial literature on this topic found that
delayed reduction and internal fixation of femoral neck fractures in patients younger
than 60 years resulted in a substantially increased rate of osteonecrosis and nonunion;
however, the effect of surgical timing on postoperative physical function and patient-
reported outcomes were mixed.6,12,17

More recent studies have shown that time to fixation is not a predictor of complications
in young adults with a femoral neck fracture.13,18 Haidukewych et al19 retrospectively
reviewed 83 femoral neck fractures in patients aged 15 to 50 years and found no
difference in the rates of osteonecrosis or nonunion in patients who underwent surgical
treatment less than or more than 24 hours from presentation. The only randomized
prospective evaluation of young adults with a displaced femoral neck fracture found that
delayed fixation did not influence the rate of nonunion or osteonecrosis.20 Multiple
studies on delayed fixation report rates of osteonecrosis and nonunion similar to those
in patients who undergo urgent treatment12,18 (Resources 2 and 3). Many of these
studies have substantial confounding variables, such as mechanism of injury, degree of
displacement, patient age, and quality of reduction and fixation methods. Time to
fixation also may be indirectly associated with a risk of complications because it may
affect the ease or quality of reduction. The exact effect of delayed fixation has not been
delineated. Timing likely is a factor; however, quality of reduction and fixation plays a
much larger role in outcomes.5,19
Open Versus Closed Reduction
Quality of reduction affects patient outcomes, regardless of surgical timing or other patient
variables.
Reduction can be performed via closed, percutaneous, or open methods.
Closed reduction is attained via manipulation of the limb under fluoroscopic guidance.
Open reduction can be performed via various surgical approaches, depending on the anatomic
area of the neck that needs to be visualized.
Guidelines on acceptable reduction are available; however, the ability of two-dimensional
fluoroscopic imaging to assess three-dimensional reduction is not ideal.

Open Versus Closed Reduction
Anatomic reduction of a displaced femoral neck fracture is one of the most important
factors under surgeon control to achieve a successful outcome. Controversy in the

14/29

literature persists regarding whether open reduction is required or closed reduction is
acceptable. Closed reduction is performed via traction and manipulation of the
extremity. Although this technique preserves the soft tissues surrounding the femoral
neck, fluoroscopic evaluation may underestimate residual displacement.21 Open
reduction affords direct visualization of the fracture fragments and assessment of the
reduction. Occasionally, percutaneous techniques may be helpful in patients in whom
near anatomic reduction is achieved via closed techniques. Ultimately, the goal is
anatomic reduction regardless of the surgical approach used because the quality of
reduction is associated with decreased complications and revision surgery rates.22-25
Extensive comminution may preclude anatomic reduction. In such patients, varus should
be avoided; however, some valgus alignment may be accepted. No retroversion or
translation should be present. Radiographs of the contralateral hip may be valuable in
determining native morphology.
Fixation Selection
Despite numerous techniques and fixation constructs that have been described for the
fixation of femoral neck fractures, a preferred implant or surgical approach does not exist.
Options include interfragmentary screw fixation, a SHS, a 95° condylar screw, an
intramedullary rod, an angled blade plate, and newer specialty devices.
Relatively horizontal fracture patterns that experience compressive forces often can be
appropriately managed with the use of cancellous interfragmentary lag screws.
Fractures that are more vertical result in higher shear stress and are better managed with the
use of a fixed-angle device, such as a SHS.

Fixation Selection
Various implants and surgical techniques are available to manage femoral neck fractures
in young adults. Options include interfragmentary screw fixation, a SHS, a 95° condylar
screw, an angled blade plate, and newer specialty devices. Each is associated with
advantages and limitations. The fracture pattern, femoral head bone quality, and
concomitant injuries play a role in selecting an appropriate construct.19,26

15/29

Horizontal fracture patterns (ie, Pauwels type I) that experience compressive forces can
be managed with the use of cancellous interfragmentary screws. These screws often are
cannulated to facilitate accurate placement. Typically, three screws are placed in a
parallel, inverted triangle configuration, with care taken to place the screws peripherally,
abutting the cortices. The inferior screw should be placed first, with care taken to
position the inferior screw adjacent to the dense calcar bone.27,28 The starting point for
the screws should be at or proximal to the lesser trochanter to avoid creation of a stress
riser, which increases the risk of subtrochanteric fracture. The addition of a screw
perpendicular to the fracture line engaging the inferior femoral head may provide
additional stability for more vertical fracture patterns.27 Radiographic analysis has
suggested that replacing the posterosuperior lag screw with a fully threaded screw may
reduce femoral neck shortening and the risk of retrotilt in nondisplaced fractures.29
More vertical fractures result in high shear forces at the fracture site. Devices such as a
SHS may be a better option to stabilize vertically oriented fracture patterns.9,30 A SHS
allows for controlled dynamic compression while reducing shear and rotational forces at
the fracture site. Similar to the use of a SHS for the management of an intertrochanteric
hip fracture, the screw should be placed in the center of or slightly inferior in the femoral
head, with a goal of achieving a tip-apex distance of less than 25 mm to prevent screw
cutout27,31 (Resource 4). The substantial insertional torque required to implant a large-
diameter lag screw may rotationally displace the reduction.27,32 Anti-rotation screws,
provisional wires, or plates can be placed before the lag screw to prevent rotational
displacement during instrumentation.27
Biomechanic studies have shown that SHS constructs provide greater mechanical
stability and resistance to shear forces relative to cancellous screws.9,30 Compared with
three cannulated screws, a SHS results in better maintenance of reduction and greater
loads to failure in cadaver models.9 Despite these in vitro differences, data do not
support the superiority of SHS versus cancellous screws.23 The success of both implants
is related to proper screw placement within the head and neck segments. Fixed-angle
proximal femur locking plate and screw devices have shown promise in biomechanical
studies but have not demonstrated similar success in vivo. Rates of osteonecrosis,

SHS implants are available in various neck-shaft angles, with multiple side plate options.
Cadaver model and biomechanical studies have shown that cyclic load and peak load to
failure are equivalent between a two-hole side plate SHS and a four-hole side plate SHS;
however, most of these studies have been performed in the context of intertrochanteric
hip fractures. A two-hole side plate may allow for smaller exposure and shorter surgical
time compared with a four-hole side plate.34,35
Surgical Approaches
Two main surgical approaches are used for open reduction of femoral neck fractures: the
direct anterior Heuter (Smith-Petersen) approach and the anterolateral Watson-Jones
approach (Figures 7 and 8).

The Watson-Jones approach provides better visualization of the basicervical neck and allows
for hardware placement via the same incision.

Surgical Approaches
The direct anterior Heuter approach (also referred to as the distal limb of the Smith-
Petersen approach) via an intermuscular, internervous interval is the best approach for
exposure of the femoral neck in the subcapital and transcervical regions (Figure 9). This
approach uses the interval between the sartorius and the tensor fascia lata superficially
and the rectus femoris–gluteus medius interval deep. This approach can be performed
with or without a rectus femoris tenotomy. Branches of the lateral femoral circumflex
artery often are encountered at the distal aspect of the approach and must be ligated.36

A separate incision is required for placement of internal fixation hardware.37 The
anterolateral Watson-Jones approach provides better visualization of the extra-capsular
proximal femur and basicervical femoral neck. This approach between the gluteus
medius and the tensor fascia lata is an intermuscular but not internervous interval;
therefore, abductor weakness may occur.38 This approach allows for reduction and
fixation via a single incision.37 (Videos 1 and 2).

Complications
Even with in situ fixation, revision surgery rates for patients with a nondisplaced fracture are
near 20% because of osteonecrosis, nonunion, and hardware failure.
Initial fracture displacement, quality of reduction, and stable fixation are the most
considerable factors influencing radiographic and clinical outcomes.

Complications
Historically, femoral neck fractures in young adults have been associated with high rates
of osteonecrosis, nonunion, and revision surgery. Outcomes have substantially improved
with an emphasis on anatomic reduction and surgical stabilization.14,15 Haidukewych et
al19 investigated the outcomes of 51 displaced femoral neck fractures in patients
younger than 50 years and reported an 82% rate of femoral head retention at a mean
follow-up of 6.6 years. Poor reduction quality was associated with osteonecrosis and
nonunion. Eighteen percent of the patients underwent conversion to total hip
arthroplasty at a mean follow-up of 7.3 years. Duckworth et al39 reported a 7.4%
nonunion rate and 11.5% osteonecrosis rate in 122 patients with a displaced femoral
neck fracture (Garden type III or type IV). At a mean follow-up of approximately 5 years,
68% of the patients had achieved fracture union. Gardner et al25 reviewed young adults
with a displaced femoral neck fracture and found that 10% of patients required revision
surgery within 6 months of the index procedure. Patients with good or excellent
reduction were substantially less likely to experience early fixation failure. Although
controversy exists regarding the optimal method of fracture fixation, clear consensus
shows that the quality of reduction is vital for successful long-term patient outcomes.40
Poor reduction quality is associated with osteonecrosis and nonunion in 75% and 50% of
patients, respectively.

Osteonecrosis is a serious and unpredictable complication that is affected by fracture
displacement, adequacy of reduction, stability of fixation, and other patient factors.
Rates are higher with displaced fractures, presumably because the femoral head vascular
supply is disrupted during injury.
Osteonecrosis occurs in as many as 20% of nondisplaced and 45% of displaced femoral neck
fractures; however, the incidence reported in the literature varies widely.
Poor reduction quality is associated with osteonecrosis.

Osteonecrosis
Osteonecrosis is a serious yet unpredictable complication that is affected by fracture
displacement, surgical timing, reduction, and patient factors. Blood supply to the
femoral head is tenuous and easily disrupted, particularly in patients with a displaced
fracture. Osteonecrosis occurs in as many as 20% of nondisplaced and 45% of displaced
femoral neck fractures; however, the incidence reported in the literature varies
widely.24,39 Osteonecrosis after femoral neck fracture may be symptomatic or
asymptomatic. Surgeons must recognize the signs and symptoms early because various
options are available for femoral head salvage. Unmanaged osteonecrosis may lead to
femoral head collapse and osteoarthritis, which often necessitates hip resurfacing, total
hip arthroplasty, or arthrodesis.13 Few studies follow patients for more than 2 years,
which is the minimum duration to understand the long-term clinical consequences of
osteonecrosis and malunion. Therefore, the true rate of revision surgery likely is higher
than that reported in the current literature.
Nonunion/Malunion
Nonunion and/or malunion occurs in 20% to 30% of patients with a femoral neck fracture.
Initial displacement, malreduction, and substantial comminution increase the risk of malunion.
Radiographic signs of nonunion include a persistently visible fracture line, change in fracture
or screw position, screw backout, or screw cutout of the femoral head.
Varus malunion results in poor abductor mechanics and gait abnormalities.
Approximately 30% of young adults with a femoral neck fracture require additional surgical
treatment for nonunion, malunion, or osteonecrosis.

Nonunion/Malunion
The rate of nonunion and malunion after internal fixation ranges from 5% to 31%, with a
higher incidence reported in patients with a displaced fracture.33,41 Malreduction, initial
displacement, and posterior comminution contribute to nonunion.40,42 Patient-specific
factors associated with nonunion include smoking, diabetes mellitus, steroid use,
advanced age, alcohol abuse, and endocrine abnormalities.24,39,43 Patients with a
nonunion or malunion typically present with groin pain and difficulty with weight bearing
several months postoperatively, which differs from patients with osteonecrosis, who
often become symptomatic later in the postoperative course.42 Radiographic signs of
nonunion include a persistently visible fracture line, a change in fracture or screw
position, screw migration, or screw cutout of the femoral head.42 Infection as the cause
of nonunion should be investigated via laboratory studies.
Varus angulation, inferior offset, and retroversion increase the risk of malunion,
nonunion, and osteonecrosis. Varus malunion may lead to hip impingement, abductor
incompetence, decreased motion, and secondary arthritis. Femoral neck shortening
results in decreased abductor tension, changing the overall mechanics of gait.24,43
Multiple studies have shown that femoral neck shortening results in inferior hip
function.24,43 Implants become more prominent with shortening, which may lead to
revision surgery for the management of symptomatic hardware.
Nonunion in young adults with a well-preserved joint and normal alignment is managed
via revision fixation with or without bone grafting. A nonunion with varus malalignment
necessitates a valgus intertrochanteric osteotomy. This procedure involves conversion of
the shearing forces to compressive forces at the fracture site, stabilizing the nonunion
and promoting healing. In addition, the osteotomy can restore femoral length and the
lever arm of the abductor mechanism.42

Deep Vein Thrombosis/Venous Thromboembolism
Femoral neck fractures in young adults often result from high-energy trauma; therefore,
associated injuries, abdominal trauma, and head trauma may result in an increased rate
of medical complications. Thromboembolic events occur at a rate of 2.8%.17 Delayed
surgical management, defined as management more than 24 hours from presentation,
is associated with an increased risk of serious inpatient adverse events, including deep
vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism.17 Aggressive mobilization and venous
thromboembolism prophylaxis may help decrease complications.
